domain: Philosophy of Physics / Quantum Foundations / Interpretive Epistemology
topic_summary: Analysis of quantum mechanics interpretive frameworks as a contested kernel. The mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics (Schrödinger equation, Born rule, Hilbert space structure) serves as a fixed substrate that different interpretive traditions read differently, yielding mutually exclusive ontological commitments about the nature of measurement, causality, and physical reality.

key_entities: Quantum formalism (Schrödinger equation, Born rule, mathematical substrate)
Copenhagen interpretation (Bohr, Heisenberg; wavefunction collapse as epistemic boundary)
Pilot Wave theory (de Broglie-Bohm; deterministic hidden variables)
Measurement apparatus (experimental interface, differently theorized across readings)
key_tensions: Determinism vs indeterminism (Many-Worlds/Pilot Wave vs Copenhagen)
Ontological commitment vs epistemic modesty (realist vs instrumentalist readings)
Local hidden variables vs nonlocality (Pilot Wave vs Copenhagen/Many-Worlds)

axiom_contradictions.basis: Copenhagen's axiom that measurement collapse is a fundamental physical process requiring a special ontological category is mutually exclusive with Many-Worlds' axiom that measurement is an entirely derivative phenomenon (decoherence). No single framework can hold both: if collapse is fundamental, branching cannot be the full story; if decoherence explains measurement, collapse is eliminated.

Copenhagen's axiom of irreducible indeterminism at measurement (Born rule as fundamental randomness) is mutually exclusive with Pilot Wave's axiom of deterministic hidden variables. No framework can hold both: accepting deterministic particle trajectories requires rejecting measurement indeterminism as fundamental.

Many-Worlds' axiom that particles do not have definite positions between measurements (only relative states in branching histories) is mutually exclusive with Pilot Wave's axiom that particles always have definite positions guided by the wave. No framework holds both: if particles always have positions, branching worlds are unnecessary; if branching is universal, definite positions are denied.

omegas.description: All three readings recover identical empirical predictions. If empirical adequacy is the sole legitimacy criterion, the interpretive contest is underdetermined by physics itself. Authority structure may collapse to philosophical preference.

Does the measurement problem (the conflict driving interpretive plurality) dissolve under decoherence-only accounts, collapsing Many-Worlds and Copenhagen into a single reading? Or does the preferred basis problem preserve the split?
